lesson.title: Lightning War: How Germany's Blitzkrieg Conquered Europe
lesson.summary: Germany's fast, coordinated attacks combining tanks, aircraft, and mobile infantry, a strategy known as blitzkrieg, overran Poland and then France in the opening phase of World War Two.
lesson.body:
Having rebuilt German military strength in defiance of the Versailles treaty and absorbed Austria and Czechoslovakia without full scale war, Hitler turned to outright invasion. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France, honoring their commitments to Poland, declared war on Germany on September 3, 1939, marking the start of World War Two in Europe.

Blitzkrieg, meaning lightning war, broke from the slow, static trench warfare that had defined World War One. German forces combined fast moving armored divisions of tanks, close air support from the Luftwaffe, and mobile infantry to punch through weak points in enemy lines, encircle defenders, and create chaos and rapid collapse before an opponent could organize an effective response.

Poland fell within about a month, its collapse hastened when the Soviet Union invaded from the east under the terms of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, a non aggression agreement Germany and the Soviet Union had signed shortly before the invasion began.

In May 1940, Germany struck France by sending armored columns through the Ardennes Forest, a densely wooded region French commanders had judged nearly impassable to tanks and therefore left lightly defended. The maneuver outflanked French and British forces, and the British Expeditionary Force along with many French troops had to be evacuated from the beaches of Dunkirk in late May and early June 1940. France signed an armistice with Germany on June 22, 1940, leaving Britain to face Germany alone. These stunning early German victories intensified pressure on the United States to decide how far it would go in supporting Britain, a question that led directly to the Lend-Lease debate.
